claim: Hair greying is a hallmark of aging generally believed to be irreversible and linked to psychological stress.
source: Hair greying is a hallmark of aging generally believed to be irreversible and linked to psychological stress.
evidence: This is a statement of general scientific belief presented in the abstract without specific supporting data in this sentence.

claim: White/grey hairs naturally regain pigmentation across sex, ethnicities, ages, and body regions.
source: Using this method, we show white/grey hairs that naturally regain pigmentation across sex, ethnicities, ages, and body regions, thereby quantitatively defining the reversibility of greying in humans.
evidence: The manuscript presents observational data from multiple participants showing hair repigmentation.

claim: Grey hairs upregulate proteins related to energy metabolism, mitochondria, and antioxidant defenses.
source: Molecularly, grey hairs upregulate proteins related to energy metabolism, mitochondria, and antioxidant defenses.
evidence: This claim is supported by proteomic analysis data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Hair greying and reversal can occur in parallel with psychological stressors.
source: Combining HPP profiling and proteomics on single hairs, we also report hair greying and reversal that can occur in parallel with psychological stressors.
evidence: The manuscript presents case studies correlating stress assessments with hair pigmentation patterns.

claim: A threshold-based mechanism is suggested for the temporary reversibility of greying.
source: To generalize these observations, we develop a computational simulation, which suggests a threshold-based mechanism for the temporary reversibility of greying.
evidence: This is based on computational modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The time of onset of hair greying varies between individuals based on genetic and other biobehavioral factors.
source: The time of onset of hair greying varies between individuals, as well as between individual hair follicles, based on genetic and other biobehavioral factors (Akin Belli et al., 2016; Bernard, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Most people experience depigmentation of a progressively large number of hair shafts from their third decade onward.
source: But most people experience depigmentation of a progressively large number of hair shafts (HSs) from their third decade onward, known as achromotrichia or canities (Panhard et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The color in pigmented hair shafts is provided by melanin granules supplied by melanocytes of the hair follicle pigmentary unit.
source: The color in pigmented HSs is provided by melanin granules, a mature form of melanosomes continuously supplied to the trichocytes of the growing hair shaft by melanocytes of the hair follicle pigmentary unit (HFPU) (Tobin, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citation.

claim: Age-related greying is thought to involve bulb and outer root sheath melanocyte stem cell exhaustion.
source: Age-related greying is thought to involve bulb and outer root sheath melanocyte stem cell (MSC) exhaustion (Commo et al., 2004; Nishimura et al., 2005), neuroendocrine alterations (Paus, 2011), and other factors, with oxidative damage to the HFPU likely being the dominant, initial driver (Arck et al., 2006; Paus, 2011; Trueb and Tobin, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous research.

claim: Oxidative damage to the HFPU is likely the dominant, initial driver of age-related greying.
source: Age-related greying is thought to involve bulb and outer root sheath melanocyte stem cell (MSC) exhaustion (Commo et al., 2004; Nishimura et al., 2005), neuroendocrine alterations (Paus, 2011), and other factors, with oxidative damage to the HFPU likely being the dominant, initial driver (Arck et al., 2006; Paus, 2011; Trueb and Tobin, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Depigmented hairs differ from pigmented hairs in growth rates, hair follicle cycle, and other biophysical properties.
source: While loss of pigmentation is the most visible change among greying hairs, depigmented hairs also differ in other ways from their pigmented counterparts (Tobin, 2015), including in their growth rates (Nagl, 1995), HF cycle, and other biophysical properties (Van Neste and Tobin, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Hair growth is an energetically demanding process relying on aerobic metabolism in the hair follicle.
source: Hair growth is an energetically demanding process (Flores et al., 2017) relying on aerobic metabolism in the HF (Williams et al., 1993), and melanosome maturation also involves the central organelle of energy metabolism, mitochondria (Basrur et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Melanosome maturation involves mitochondria.
source: Hair growth is an energetically demanding process (Flores et al., 2017) relying on aerobic metabolism in the HF (Williams et al., 1993), and melanosome maturation also involves the central organelle of energy metabolism, mitochondria (Basrur et al., 2003; Zhang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Mitochondria likely contribute to oxidative stress within the hair follicle.
source: Moreover, mitochondria likely contribute to oxidative stress within the HF (Lemasters et al., 2017), providing converging evidence that white hairs may exhibit specific alterations in mitochondrial energy metabolism.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and logical inference.

claim: White hairs may exhibit specific alterations in mitochondrial energy metabolism.
source: Moreover, mitochondria likely contribute to oxidative stress within the HF (Lemasters et al., 2017), providing converging evidence that white hairs may exhibit specific alterations in mitochondrial energy metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited evidence about mitochondrial function.

claim: Hair greying is generally considered a progressive and irreversible age-related process, with the exclusion of alopecia areata.
source: Although hair greying is generally considered a progressive and irreversible age-related process, with the exclusion of alopecia areata (McBride and Bergfeld, 1990), cases of drug- and mineral deficiency-induced depigmentation or repigmentation of hair have been reported (Kavak et al., 2005; Kobayashi et al., 2014; Komagamine et al., 2013; Reynolds et al., 1989; Ricci et al., 2016; Sieve, 1941; Yoon et al., 2003) reflecting the influence of environmental inputs into HFPU function (Paus et al., 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Cases of drug- and mineral deficiency-induced depigmentation or repigmentation of hair have been reported.
source: Although hair greying is generally considered a progressive and irreversible age-related process, with the exclusion of alopecia areata (McBride and Bergfeld, 1990), cases of drug- and mineral deficiency-induced depigmentation or repigmentation of hair have been reported (Kavak et al., 2005; Kobayashi et al., 2014; Komagamine et al., 2013; Reynolds et al., 1989; Ricci et al., 2016; Sieve, 1941; Yoon et al., 2003) reflecting the influence of environmental inputs into HFPU function (Paus et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous case reports.

claim: The hair shaft represents a bioarchive of recent exposures.
source: Because most hairs are continually growing from a living hair follicle, sensitive to changing physiological conditions, into a hardened hair shaft external to the body that retains stable molecular traces of these conditions, the hair shaft represents a bioarchive of recent exposures (Kalliokoski et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and logical reasoning about hair structure.

claim: Spontaneous repigmentation can be pharmacologically induced.
source: While spontaneous repigmentation can be pharmacologically induced, its natural occurrence in unmedicated individuals is rare and has only been reported in a few single-patient case studies (Comaish, 1972; Navarini and Trüeb, 2010; O'Sullivan et al., 2021; Tobin and Cargnello, 1993; Tobin and Paus, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Natural occurrence of spontaneous repigmentation in unmedicated individuals is rare and has only been reported in a few single-patient case studies.
source: While spontaneous repigmentation can be pharmacologically induced, its natural occurrence in unmedicated individuals is rare and has only been reported in a few single-patient case studies (Comaish, 1972; Navarini and Trüeb, 2010; O'Sullivan et al., 2021; Tobin and Cargnello, 1993; Tobin and Paus, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous case studies.

claim: The reversal of hair greying has not been quantitatively examined in a cohort of healthy adults, in parallel with molecular factors and psychosocial exposures.
source: The reversal of hair greying has not been quantitatively examined in a cohort of healthy adults, in parallel with molecular factors and psychosocial exposures.
evidence: This is a statement about the gap in existing literature.

claim: In humans, psychological stress accelerates biological aging as measured by telomere length.
source: In humans, psychological stress accelerates biological aging as measured by telomere length (Epel et al., 2004; Puterman et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In mice, psychological stress and the stress mediator norepinephrine acutely causes depigmentation.
source: In mice, psychological stress and the stress mediator norepinephrine acutely causes depigmentation (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Greying in both mice and humans has been shown to be a relatively irreversible phenomenon driven in part by a depletion of melanocyte stem cells.
source: However, greying in both mice and humans has been shown to be a relatively irreversible phenomenon driven in part by a depletion of melanocyte stem cells, although some stem cells and transient amplifying cells do remain (Trueb and Tobin, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Some melanocyte stem cells and transient amplifying cells remain in greying hair follicles.
source: However, greying in both mice and humans has been shown to be a relatively irreversible phenomenon driven in part by a depletion of melanocyte stem cells, although some stem cells and transient amplifying cells do remain (Trueb and Tobin, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Recent evidence suggests hair growth and pigmentation changes in response to stress in humans.
source: In humans, recent evidence suggests hair growth and pigmentation changes in response to stress (Peters et al., 2017), but this relationship, along with reversal of greying, remain insufficiently understood.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The relationship between stress and hair greying, along with reversal of greying, remain insufficiently understood.
source: In humans, recent evidence suggests hair growth and pigmentation changes in response to stress (Peters et al., 2017), but this relationship, along with reversal of greying, remain insufficiently understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The paucity of quantitative data in humans is mostly due to the lack of sensitive methods to precisely correlate stressful psychobiological processes with hair pigmentation and greying events at the single-follicle level.
source: The paucity of quantitative data in humans is mostly due to the lack of sensitive methods to precisely correlate stressful psychobiological processes with hair pigmentation and greying events at the single-follicle level.
evidence: This is an inference about the reasons for limited data in the field.

claim: Rare repigmentation events are more likely to occur in the early stages of canities.
source: Because previous literature suggests that rare repigmentation events are more likely to occur in the early stages of canities (Van Neste and Tobin, 2004), the current study focuses primarily on pigmentation events in young to middle-aged participants.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The current study focuses primarily on pigmentation events in young to middle-aged participants.
source: Because previous literature suggests that rare repigmentation events are more likely to occur in the early stages of canities (Van Neste and Tobin, 2004), the current study focuses primarily on pigmentation events in young to middle-aged participants.
evidence: This is a statement about the study design.

claim: A total of 14 individuals (seven females, seven males), mean age 35 ± 13 (SD, range: 9–65), were recruited.
source: A total of 14 individuals (seven females, seven males), mean age 35 ± 13 (SD, range: 9–65), were recruited.
evidence: This is demographic data from the study.

claim: Only plucked hairs with follicular tissue attached (excluding broken hairs) were used in analyses.
source: Only plucked hairs with follicular tissue attached (excluding broken hairs) were used in analyses to enable the interpretation of the direction of pigmentation – transition if the HS tip is dark and the root white, reversal if the HS tip is white and the root dark.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the study.

claim: The typical age of onset for greying or canities corresponds to the participant age range in this study.
source: While the participant age range does not capture the typical range of an aged population, it provides an opportune window to examine the beginning of the aging process as it corresponds to the typical age of onset for greying or canities (Tobin, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Hair follicles manifest stochastic hair-to-hair heterogeneity similar to that seen between individual cells in aging organs.
source: The hair follicles also manifest stochastic hair-to-hair heterogeneity similar to that seen between individual cells in aging organs (Bernard, 2012; van Deursen, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Some hair follicles reach the end of their pigmented life even in relatively young individuals as a result of stochastic processes.
source: For this reason, likely as a result of stochastic processes similar to those that drive cellular heterogeneity in gene expression, some HFs reach the end of their pigmented life even in relatively young individuals.
evidence: This is an inference based on cited research about stochastic processes.

claim: Dark hairs contain melanin granules dispersed throughout the hair cortex.
source: Whereas dark hairs contain melanin granules dispersed throughout the hair cortex when observed by electron microscopy, white hairs from the same individuals show a near complete (>98%) absence of melanin, with the few retained melanin granules, when present, being smaller, less dense, and at times vacuolated, a potential response to oxidative stress (Tobin, 2009; Figure 1E–I, see Figure 1—figure supplement 5 for high-resolution images of mature melanosomes).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: White hairs from the same individuals show a near complete (>98%) absence of melanin.
source: Whereas dark hairs contain melanin granules dispersed throughout the hair cortex when observed by electron microscopy, white hairs from the same individuals show a near complete (>98%) absence of melanin, with the few retained melanin granules, when present, being smaller, less dense, and at times vacuolated, a potential response to oxidative stress (Tobin, 2009; Figure 1E–I, see Figure 1—figure supplement 5 for high-resolution images of mature melanosomes).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The few retained melanin granules in white hairs are smaller, less dense, and at times vacuolated.
source: Whereas dark hairs contain melanin granules dispersed throughout the hair cortex when observed by electron microscopy, white hairs from the same individuals show a near complete (>98%) absence of melanin, with the few retained melanin granules, when present, being smaller, less dense, and at times vacuolated, a potential response to oxidative stress (Tobin, 2009; Figure 1E–I, see Figure 1—figure supplement 5 for high-resolution images of mature melanosomes).
evidence: This is supported by electron microscopy data and a citation.

claim: Vacuolated melanin granules are a potential response to oxidative stress.
source: Whereas dark hairs contain melanin granules dispersed throughout the hair cortex when observed by electron microscopy, white hairs from the same individuals show a near complete (>98%) absence of melanin, with the few retained melanin granules, when present, being smaller, less dense, and at times vacuolated, a potential response to oxidative stress (Tobin, 2009; Figure 1E–I, see Figure 1—figure supplement 5 for high-resolution images of mature melanosomes).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: A total of 323 proteins (>75% of samples) were extracted and quantified from single 2-cm-long hair shaft segments in Experiment 1.
source: In the first experiment, we were able to extract and quantify 323 proteins (>75% of samples) from single 2-cm-long HS segments.
evidence: This is a methodological result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: White hairs contained several differentially enriched (upregulated) or depleted (downregulated) proteins compared to dark hair shafts.
source: Compared to dark HS collected at the same time from the same individuals, white hairs contained several differentially enriched (upregulated) or depleted (downregulated) proteins (Figure 1J–K see Supplementary file 1 for complete list) on which we performed GO (Gene Ontology) and KEGG (Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes) enrichment analysis and explored their protein-protein interaction networks (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data presented in figures and supplementary files.

claim: The protein networks for both downregulated and upregulated proteins contain significantly more interactions than expected by chance (p<0.00001).
source: The protein networks for both downregulated (<0.8 fold, n = 23) and upregulated (>1.5 fold, n = 67) proteins contain significantly more interactions than expected by chance (p<0.00001, observed vs expected protein-protein interactions).
evidence: This is a statistical result from protein-protein interaction network analysis.

claim: A large fraction (34.3%) of upregulated proteins in white hairs was related to ribosome function, protein processing, and associated cytoskeletal proteins.
source: A large fraction (34.3%) of upregulated proteins in white hairs was related to ribosome function, protein processing, and associated cytoskeletal proteins.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from proteomic analysis.

claim: Of all upregulated proteins in white hairs, 26.8% were known mitochondrial proteins.
source: Of all upregulated proteins in white hairs, 26.8% were known mitochondrial proteins, based on MitoCarta2.0 and others sources (Calvo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from proteomic analysis using established databases.

claim: White hairs contained more proteins involved in glucose and lipid metabolism.
source: White hairs also contained more proteins involved in glucose (glucose 6-phosphate dehydrogenase, G6PD; phosphoglycerate kinase 1, PGK1) and lipid metabolism located in either the mitochondria or cytoplasm (fatty acid synthase, FASN; acyl-CoA thioesterase 7, ACOT7; mitochondrial trifunctional enzyme subunit beta, HADHB) or in peroxisomes (acyl-CoA acyltransferase 1, ACAA1).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: The metabolic remodeling in white hairs is consistent with the established role of mitochondria and metabolic regulation of hair growth and maintenance in animal models.
source: The metabolic remodeling in white hairs is consistent with the established role of mitochondria and metabolic regulation of hair growth and maintenance in animal models (Flores et al., 2017; Kloepper et al., 2015; Singh et al., 2018; Vidali et al., 2014), and possibly consistent with hair anomalies reported in human patients with mitochondrial disease (Silengo et al., 2003).
evidence: This is an inference based on the current data and citations to previous research.

claim: Several lysosomal proteins (PLD3, CTSD, HEXB, and LAMP1) were downregulated in white hairs.
source: In line with the lysosomal origin of melanosomes that are largely absent in depigmented HS (Slominski et al., 2005), several lysosomal proteins (PLD3, CTSD, HEXB, and LAMP1) were downregulated in white hairs, consistent with previous literature (Franklin et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data and citations to previous research.

claim: White hair shafts showed a depletion of six main keratins.
source: White hair shafts also showed a depletion of six main keratins (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2), likely because greying can affect the nature of keratinocytes proliferation (Van Neste and Tobin, 2004), of proteins associated with exocytosis, such as ITIH4 and APOH (potentially involved in the secretion of melanosomes from melanocytes to keratinocytes), as well as proteins associated with mitochondrial calcium transmembrane transport.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data presented in figures.

claim: Calcium exchange between mitochondria and the melanosome is required for melanin pigment production in melanocytes.
source: Interestingly, calcium exchange between mitochondria and the melanosome is required for melanin pigment production in melanocytes (Zhang et al., 2019), and calcium signaling promotes melanin transfer between melanosomes and keratinocytes (Singh et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Canities-affected white hair follicles showed upregulation of antioxidant proteins, specifically those localized to mitochondria and cytoplasm (SOD1, PRDX2).
source: Finally, canities-affected white HFs also showed upregulation of antioxidant proteins, specifically those localized to mitochondria and cytoplasm (superoxide dismutase 1, SOD1; peroxiredoxin 2, PRDX2), in line with the role of oxidative stress in HS depigmentation (Arck et al., 2006; Wood et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data and citations to previous research.

claim: In Experiment 2, a total of 192 proteins (≥3 samples) were quantified from 1cm-long hair shaft segments.
source: In this experiment, a total of 192 proteins (≥3 samples) were quantified from 1cm-long HS segments.
evidence: This is a methodological result from the proteomic analysis.

claim: Experiment 2 showed a similar trend as Experiment 1 toward a preferential overexpression of proteins with greying (55% upregulated vs 29% downregulated in white hair shafts).
source: This dataset showed a similar trend as the first analysis toward a preferential overexpression of proteins with greying (55% upregulated vs 29% downregulated in white HS) (Figure 1L–M, see Supplementary file 2 for a complete list).
evidence: This is a quantitative result from proteomic analysis.

claim: The most highly upregulated proteins in Experiment 2 included mitochondrial components such as VDAC1, ATP5A1, and PHB2.
source: The most highly upregulated proteins included mitochondrial components such as the voltage-dependent anion channel 1 (VDAC1), a subunit of ATP synthase (ATP5A1), and a regulator of mitochondrial respiratory chain assembly (Prohibitin-2, PHB2).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: The antioxidant enzyme SOD1 was enriched in white relative to dark hair shafts in Experiment 2.
source: Again, the antioxidant enzyme SOD1 was enriched in white relative to dark HSs.
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: Housekeeping proteins, including keratins and keratin-associated proteins, were not downregulated in white hairs, but generally unchanged or slightly upregulated.
source: This confirmed that the housekeeping proteins, including keratins and keratin-associated proteins, were not downregulated in white hairs, but generally unchanged or slightly upregulated.
evidence: This is supported by iBAQ data analysis.

claim: Upregulated proteins formed a coherent protein-protein interactions cluster (p<0.00001).
source: Moreover, as a whole, upregulated proteins formed a coherent protein-protein interactions cluster (p<0.00001) and pathway analysis again showed a significant enrichment of carbon metabolism, glycolysis/glucogenesis, pyruvate metabolism, and amino acid synthesis pathways in white relative to dark HS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a statistical result from protein-protein interaction network analysis.

claim: Pathway analysis showed a significant enrichment of carbon metabolism, glycolysis/glucogenesis, pyruvate metabolism, and amino acid synthesis pathways in white relative to dark hair shafts.
source: Moreover, as a whole, upregulated proteins formed a coherent protein-protein interactions cluster (p<0.00001) and pathway analysis again showed a significant enrichment of carbon metabolism, glycolysis/glucogenesis, pyruvate metabolism, and amino acid synthesis pathways in white relative to dark HS (Figure 1—figure supplement 3, Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: Proteins downregulated in white hair shafts were related to cholesterol metabolism, complement-coagulation cascades, and secretory processes shared with immune/inflammatory pathways.
source: On the other hand, proteins downregulated in white HSs were related to cholesterol metabolism, complement-coagulation cascades, and secretory processes shared with immune/inflammatory pathways (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is supported by pathway enrichment analysis.

claim: The downregulation of secretory pathways is consistent with reduced transfer of pigmented melanosomes from the melanocytes to the keratinocytes.
source: The downregulation of secretory pathways is again consistent with reduced transfer of pigmented melanosomes from the melanocytes to the keratinocytes.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data.

claim: A PLS-DA multivariate model provided adequate separation of white vs dark hair shafts.
source: To verify the robustness of these findings using an alternative analytical approach, we built a simple partial least square discriminant analysis (PLS-DA) multivariate model, which provided adequate separation of white vs dark HS (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is supported by multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: 13 proteins were undetectable in any of the dark hair shafts but consistently present in white hair shafts.
source: Interestingly, we also identified 13 proteins that were undetectable in any of the dark HS (either not expressed, or below the detection limit), but consistently present in white HS (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This is supported by proteomic data.

claim: These 13 proteins are either newly induced or experience a substantial upregulation with greying (fold change tending toward infinity).
source: These proteins are either newly induced or experience a substantial upregulation with greying (fold change tending toward infinity).
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data.

claim: Functional enrichment analysis for the 13 induced proteins showed significant enrichment for aging-related metabolic pathways: glycolysis/glucogenesis, carbon, pyruvate, and cysteine and methionine metabolism (all p<0.001).
source: A separate functional enrichment analysis for these induced proteins also showed significant enrichment for the same aging-related metabolic pathways as for the upregulated protein list: glycolysis/glucogenesis, carbon, pyruvate, and cysteine and methionine metabolism (all p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by functional enrichment analysis.

claim: The converging proteomics data support a multifactorial process directly implicating metabolic changes in human hair greying.
source: These converging proteomics data, which are consistent with previous findings (Franklin et al., 2020), support a multifactorial process directly implicating metabolic changes in human hair greying (Paus, 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data and citations to previous research.

claim: Given that metabolic pathways exhibit plasticity, human hair greying could be, at least temporarily, reversible.
source: Moreover, given that metabolic pathways are rapidly and extensively remodeled by environmental and neuroendocrine factors – that is, they naturally exhibit plasticity – these data build upon previous proteomic evidence to show that human hair greying could be, at least temporarily, reversible.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data and knowledge about metabolic plasticity.

claim: White hairs naturally reverted to their former dark pigmented state in several occasions in healthy unmedicated individuals.
source: Our analysis of HPPs in healthy unmedicated individuals revealed several occasions whereby white hairs naturally reverted to their former dark pigmented state.
evidence: This is supported by observational data from the study.

claim: The reversal of greying was observed in both female and male individuals, ranging from a prepubescent child to adults (age range 9–39 years).
source: Here, we document the reversal of greying along the same HS in both female and male individuals, ranging from a prepubescent child to adults (age range 9–39 years), and across individuals of different ethnic backgrounds (1 Hispanic, 8 Caucasian, 1 Asian).
evidence: This is demographic data from the study.

claim: The reversal of greying was observed across individuals of different ethnic backgrounds (1 Hispanic, 8 Caucasian, 1 Asian).
source: Here, we document the reversal of greying along the same HS in both female and male individuals, ranging from a prepubescent child to adults (age range 9–39 years), and across individuals of different ethnic backgrounds (1 Hispanic, 8 Caucasian, 1 Asian).
evidence: This is demographic data from the study.

claim: The reversal of greying was observed across frontal, temporal, and parietal regions of the scalp, as well as across other corporeal regions, including pubic and beard hairs.
source: This phenomenon was observed across frontal, temporal, and parietal regions of the scalp (Figure 2A), as well as across other corporeal regions, including pubic (Figure 2B) and beard hairs (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by observational data and images from the study.

claim: The existence of white hair shafts undergoing repigmentation across ages, sexes, ethnicity, and corporeal regions documents the reversibility of hair greying as a general phenomenon not limited to scalp hairs.
source: The existence of white HS undergoing repigmentation across ages, sexes, ethnicity, and corporeal regions documents the reversibility of hair greying as a general phenomenon not limited to scalp hairs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observational data.

claim: The repigmentation phenomenon is limited to rare, isolated hair follicles.
source: Nevertheless, we note that this phenomenon is limited to rare, isolated hair follicles.
evidence: This is an observation from the study.

claim: Over an active recruitment period of 2.5 years, only 14 participants with repigmentation were identified, indicative of the rarity of this phenomenon.
source: Over an active recruitment period of 2.5 years, we were only able to identify 14 participants, indicative of the rarity of this phenomenon.
evidence: This is data about recruitment from the study.

claim: More complex hair pigmentation patterns with double transitions and reversions in the same hair shaft were observed in both directions.
source: Moreover, more complex HPPs with double transitions and reversions in the same HS were observed in both directions: HS undergoing greying followed by rapid reversal (Figure 2D), and repigmentation rapidly followed by greying (Figure 2E).
evidence: This is supported by observational data and images from the study.

claim: Both double transition patterns must have occurred over the course of a single anagen (growth) phase in the hair growth cycle.
source: Importantly, both patterns must have occurred over the course of a single anagen (growth) phase in the hair growth cycle, implicating cellular mechanisms within the HFPU.
evidence: This is an inference based on knowledge of hair growth cycles and the observed data.

claim: The current study provides the first quantitative account of the natural and transitory reversibility of hair greying in humans.
source: Greatly extending previous case studies of these rare hair repigmentation events, the current study provides the first quantitative account of the natural and transitory reversibility of hair greying in humans.
evidence: This is a statement about the novelty of the study's contribution.

claim: Repigmentation must take place within weeks to months after greying has occurred in double transition hair shafts.
source: In double transition HS with three segments, repigmentation must take place within weeks to months after greying has occurred, producing three distinct segments present on the same hair strand (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is an inference based on hair growth rates and observed patterns.

claim: A proposed mechanism for repigmentation events involves the activation and differentiation of a subpopulation of immature melanocytes located in a reservoir outside of the hair follicle bulb in the upper outer root sheath.
source: A proposed mechanism for such repigmentation events involve the activation and differentiation of a subpopulation of immature melanocytes located in a reservoir outside of the hair follicle bulb in the upper outer root sheath (Van Neste and Tobin, 2004), or more likely from transient amplifying melanoblast cells that migrate along the outer root sheath to the interfollicular epidermis (Birlea et al., 2017).
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on citations to previous research.

claim: Across individuals, the rates of depigmentation in greying hairs ranged widely from 0.3 to 23.5 units of hair optical density per day, corresponding to between 0.2% and 14.4% loss of hair color per day.
source: Across individuals, assuming a scalp hair growth rate of 1 cm/month (LeBeau et al., 2011), the rates of depigmentation in greying hairs ranged widely from 0.3 to 23.5 units of hair optical density (scale of 0–255 units) per day, corresponding to between 0.2% and 14.4% loss of hair color per day (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the study based on hair pigmentation pattern analysis.

claim: The rate at which hair shafts regain pigmentation during reversal was 0.1–42.5 units per day, which is similar (~30% faster on average) to the rate of greying.
source: The rate at which HS regain pigmentation during reversal was 0.1–42.5 units per day, which is similar (~30% faster on average) to the rate of greying (Cohen's d = 0.15, p=0.59) (Figure 2J).
evidence: This is quantitative data from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: The fastest measured transitioning hairs grey and undergo full reversal in ~3–7 days (median: ~3 months).
source: Given these rates, the fastest measured transitioning hairs grey and undergo full reversal in ~3–7 days (median: ~3 months).
evidence: This is a calculation based on measured rates from the study.

claim: Repigmentation of white human hair shafts occurs within the same time frame and at least as rapidly as the process of greying itself.
source: Thus, rather than drifting back toward the original color, repigmentation of white human HS occurs within the same time frame and at least as rapidly as the process of greying itself.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rate data from the study.

claim: Reversal/repigmentation may reflect the action of as yet unknown local or systemic factors acting on the hair follicle pigmentary unit within a time frame of days to weeks.
source: These data also suggest that reversal/repigmentation may reflect the action of as yet unknown local or systemic factors acting on the HFPU within a time frame of days to weeks.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observed data.

claim: In a 35-year-old female participant, three two-colored hairs exhibited dark-to-white greying with strikingly similar trajectories (r = 0.76–0.82).
source: In a first 35-year-old female participant with dark brown hair, three two-colored hairs were identified at a single instance of collection. Notably, all three hairs exhibited dark-to-white greying. Moreover, when the HPPs of the three hairs were quantified and plotted, the HPPs followed strikingly similar greying trajectories (r = 0.76–0.82) marked by a similar time of onset of greying, similar HPP intermittent fluctuations (note the rise ~10 cm), and a similar time point where all hairs become fully depigmented (~15 cm) (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is observational data from the study with quantitative correlation analysis.

claim: A permutation test on the similarity of the color trajectories of three hairs from one participant yielded p=0.032, suggesting possible synchrony between different hair shafts.
source: A permutation test on the similarity of the color trajectories yielded p=0.032, suggesting possible synchrony between different HSs.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: In a 37-year-old female participant, two transition hairs revealed strikingly similar trajectories (r = 0.80) undergoing spontaneous reversal in a near-synchronous manner (p<0.001).
source: In a 37-year-old female participant with brown hair, two transition hairs were identified. The HPPs for both hairs revealed strikingly similar trajectories (r = 0.80), in this case undergoing spontaneous reversal in a near-synchronous manner upon alignment (p<0.001 when considering hairs transitioning in either direction, and similarly, p<0.001 considering only hairs transitioning from white to dark, Figure 3B).
evidence: This is observational data from the study with statistical analysis.

claim: Candidate humoral hair pigmentation modulators that could create synchrony in greying or repigmenting hairs include neuropeptides, redox balance, and steroid or catecholamine hormones.
source: Candidate humoral hair pigmentation modulators that could create synchrony in greying or repigmenting hairs include neuropeptides, redox balance, and steroid or catecholamine hormones (Hardman et al., 2015; Paus et al., 2014; Tobin and Kauser, 2005; Zhang et al., 2020) that can directly regulate the human HFPU (Paus, 2011), impact intrafollicular clock activity (Hardman et al., 2015), or regulate the expression of other melanotropic neurohormones in the human HFPU such as α-MSH, ß-endorphin, and TRH (Gáspár et al., 2011).
evidence: This is speculation based on citations to previous research.

claim: A systematic survey of a 35-year-old Caucasian male's scalp yielded five two-colored hair shafts, all of which exhibited reversal.
source: A systematic survey of two-colored hairs on the scalp of a 35-year-old Caucasian male with auburn hair color over a 2-day period yielded five two-colored HS from the frontal and temporal scalp regions. Again, two-colored hairs could either exhibit depigmentation or reversal. Unexpectedly, all HS exhibited reversal.
evidence: This is observational data from the study.

claim: All five hair shafts from the 35-year-old male underwent reversal around the same time period.
source: HPP analysis further showed that all HS underwent reversal of greying around the same time period.
evidence: This is observational data from the study.

claim: The reversal of greying for all hairs from the 35-year-old male coincided closely with the decline in stress and a 1-month period of lowest stress over the past year following a 2-week vacation.
source: The reversal of greying for all hairs coincided closely with the decline in stress and a 1-month period of lowest stress over the past year (0 on a scale of 0–10) following a 2-week vacation (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is observational data correlating hair pigmentation patterns with retrospective stress assessments.

claim: In a 30-year-old Asian female, the increase in stress corresponded in time with the complete but reversible hair greying.
source: Strikingly, the quantitative life stress assessment over the last year revealed a specific 2-month period associated with an objective life stressor (marital conflict and separation, concluded with relocation) where the participant rated her perceived stress as the highest (9–10 out of 10) over the past year. The increase in stress corresponded in time with the complete but reversible hair greying (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is observational data correlating hair pigmentation patterns with retrospective stress assessments.

claim: The association between stress and hair greying/reversal in the 30-year-old Asian female was highly significant (p=0.007).
source: This association was highly significant (p=0.007) based on our permutation test.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the study.

claim: Life stress is the likely preceding cause of the hair shaft greying and reversal dynamics observed in the 30-year-old Asian female.
source: Given the low statistical probability that these events are related by chance, life stress is the likely preceding cause of these HS greying and reversal dynamics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statistical analysis and temporal correlation.

claim: Six segments (two dark, two white, two reverted) of a single hair shaft were dissected and their proteomes quantified, producing a longitudinal, single-hair, proteomic signature containing 301 proteins.
source: To assess whether rapid greying and reversal events among a single hair are molecularly similar or distinct to those described in the two proteomics experiments above, we dissected six segments (two dark, two white, two reverted) of the single HS in Figure 3D and quantified their proteomes as part of Experiment 2. This produced a longitudinal, single-hair, proteomic signature (Figure 3E) containing 301 proteins quantified in ≥2 of the six segments.
evidence: This is methodological and quantitative data from the proteomic analysis.

claim: In the PLS-DA model of six hair segments, both dark segments clustered together, while white and reverted segments clustered in separate topological spaces.
source: To examine how the proteome as a whole is altered through the greying and reversal transitions associated with psychosocial stress levels, we generated a PLS-DA model with all six segments. Both dark segments clustered together, with similar values on both first and second principal components. The white and reverted segments clustered in separate topological spaces (Figure 3F).
evidence: This is a result from multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: Greying was associated with a positive shift largely along the first component (Component 1) of the PLS-DA model.
source: Greying was associated with a positive shift largely along the first component (Component 1), whereas reversal was associated with a negative shift on the second component (Component 2) and a more modest negative shift in Component 1.
evidence: This is a result from multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: Reversal was associated with a negative shift on the second component (Component 2) and a more modest negative shift in Component 1 of the PLS-DA model.
source: Greying was associated with a positive shift largely along the first component (Component 1), whereas reversal was associated with a negative shift on the second component (Component 2) and a more modest negative shift in Component 1.
evidence: This is a result from multivariate statistical analysis.

claim: Component 1 (associated with greying) in the single-hair analysis mapped to carbon metabolism, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and Kreb's cycle as the top three functional categories.
source: In gene set enrichment analysis of Component 1 (greying), the top three functional categories were carbon metabolism, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and Kreb's cycle (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a result from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: Component 2 (reversal)-associated proteins mapped to pathways related to the complement activation cascade, infectious processes, and Parkinson's and Huntington's disease.
source: Component 2 (reversal)-associated proteins exhibited distinct trajectories either peaking in the first white segment or upon reversal (Figure 3I) and mapped to pathways related to the complement activation cascade, infectious processes, and Parkinson's and Huntington's disease (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is a result from functional enrichment analysis.

claim: The reversal of greying at the single-hair level is not associated with a complete reversal in the molecular composition of the hair shaft.
source: These data indicate that the reversal of greying at the single-hair level is not associated with a complete reversal in the molecular composition of the HS.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data from the single-hair analysis.

claim: Some of the proteomic changes in hair greying are enduring despite successful repigmentation.
source: Rather, some of the proteomic changes in hair greying are enduring despite successful repigmentation.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data from the single-hair analysis.

claim: Five proteins were consistently upregulated between experiments 1 and 2: CPT1A, ACOT7, SOD1, CFL1, and PGK1.
source: Five proteins were consistently upregulated between experiments 1 and 2. These include three well-defined resident mitochondrial proteins involved in lipid metabolism: CPT1A, which imports fatty acids into mitochondria Schlaepfer and Joshi, 2020; ACOT7, which hydrolyzes long-chain fatty acyl-CoA esters in the mitochondrial matrix and cytoplasm (Bekeova et al., 2019); and SOD1, which dismutates superoxide anion into hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) in the mitochondrial intermembrane space (Okado-Matsumoto and Fridovich, 2001). The other two proteins include the actin-depolymerizing protein cofilin-1 (CFL1) and the core glycolysis enzyme phosphoglycerate kinase 1 (PGK1) (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is a result from comparing proteomic datasets across experiments.

claim: All five proteins validated across both proteomic experiments are linked to mitochondrial energy metabolism.
source: Thus, all five proteins validated across both experiments are linked to mitochondrial energy metabolism, implicating mitochondrial remodeling as a feature of hair greying.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic data and knowledge of protein function.

claim: All five consistently upregulated proteins have been linked to the biology of melanocytes.
source: Interestingly, all five proteins have also been linked to the biology of melanocytes (Bracalente et al., 2018; Morvan et al., 2012; Oh et al., 2014; Sumantran et al., 2015; Sung et al., 2016), the source of pigment in the HFPU.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Analysis of iBAQ data confirmed the upregulation of the five mitochondrial proteins and the absence of substantial changes in the keratins.
source: Analysis of the intensity based on absolute quantification (iBAQ) data confirmed the upregulation of these five mitochondrial proteins, and the absence of substantial changes in the keratins.
evidence: This is a result from iBAQ data analysis.

claim: Hair shaft proteome profiling may provide a retrospective access to some aspect of melanocyte metabolism.
source: Together, these data suggest that HS proteome profiling may provide a retrospective access to some aspect of melanocyte metabolism, which opens new possibilities to study HF aging biology.
evidence: This is speculation based on the proteomic findings.

claim: The upregulation of mitochondrial components unlikely reflects a bulk increase in total mitochondrial content.
source: Since the observed proteomic signatures are related to specific metabolic pathways rather than the typical high-abundance mitochondrial housekeeping proteins, we reasoned that the upregulation of these mitochondrial components unlikely reflects a bulk increase in total mitochondrial content.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of the upregulated proteins.

claim: Both white and dark hair shafts contain similarly high levels of mtDNA.
source: To investigate this point using an independent method, we quantified mitochondrial DNA (mtDNA) abundance in human HSs by real-time qPCR. Both white and dark HSs contain similarly high levels of mtDNA (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: The same mtDNA levels were found in the follicles of white and dark hairs.
source: The same was true in the follicles of the same hairs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by qPCR data.

claim: The similar mtDNA levels between dark and white hair shafts and hair follicles increases the likelihood that the reported proteomic changes reflect the induction of specific metabolic pathways rather than bulk increase in mitochondrial mass.
source: The similar mtDNA levels between dark and white HSs and HFs increases the likelihood that the reported proteomic changes reflect the induction of specific metabolic pathways associated with hair greying rather than bulk increase in mitochondrial mass.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mtDNA data and proteomic findings.

claim: White hair shafts showed consistent upregulation of carbon metabolism and amino acid biosynthesis, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and general metabolic pathways across all datasets.
source: To identify a general proteomic signature of greying hair, we compiled the enrichment scores for KEGG pathways across all datasets (Figure 4E). Consistent with the function of the individual proteins identified in both group comparisons (Experiments 1 and 2) and the multi-segment double-transition hair, white HS showed consistent upregulation of carbon metabolism and amino acid biosynthesis, glycolysis/gluconeogenesis, and general metabolic pathways relevant to aging biology (Wiley and Campisi, 2016).
evidence: This is a result from pathway enrichment analysis across datasets.

claim: Computing the cross-correlations for each protein pair revealed four main clusters among the hair shaft proteome.
source: In relation to hair biology in general, our data adds to previous efforts (Franklin et al., 2020) and provides a quantitative map of the co-expression among keratin and non-keratin HS proteins across dark and white hairs (Figure 4F). Computing the cross-correlations for each protein pair revealed four main clusters among the HS proteome (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a result from correlation analysis of proteomic data.

claim: Keratins were well-represented and constituted the main GO biological processes category for three of the four protein clusters.
source: As expected for hair, keratins were well-represented and constituted the main GO biological processes category for three of the four clusters.
evidence: This is a result from functional enrichment analysis of protein clusters.

claim: The top KEGG categories for protein clusters included glycolysis and estrogen signaling pathways, which showed strong co-expression with each other.
source: The top KEGG categories included glycolysis and estrogen signaling pathways, which also showed strong co-expression with each other, highlighting potential interaction among endocrino-metabolic processes in relation to human hair pigmentation.
evidence: This is a result from pathway enrichment and correlation analysis.

claim: The identification of several non-keratin metabolism-related proteins in the hair shaft opens new opportunities to investigate greying pathobiology and to non-invasively access past molecular and metabolic changes in the aging hair follicle pigmentary unit.
source: In general, the identification of several non-keratin metabolism-related proteins in the HS opens new opportunities to investigate greying pathobiology and to non-invasively access past molecular and metabolic changes that have occurred in the aging HFPU of the dynamically growing hair.
evidence: This is speculation about future research opportunities based on the findings.

claim: A mathematical model was developed to simulate hair greying trajectories across the human lifespan.
source: Finally, to narrow the range of plausible mechanisms for the observed age-related greying and reversal events, we developed a simulation model of HPPs. Greying dynamics of an individual's hair population (~100,000 hairs) across the average 80 year lifespan cannot practically be measured. In the absence of such data, we propose here a mathematical model to simulate hair greying trajectories across the human lifespan (Figure 5A, available online, see Materials and methods for details) as has been attempted previously for hair growth cycles (Halloy et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a description of the computational modeling approach.

claim: The onset of human hair greying is not yet underway and rarely begins in childhood.
source: As basic tenets for this model, it is established that (i) the onset of human hair greying is not yet underway and rarely begins in childhood, (ii) greying routinely starts between 20 and 50 years of age, (iii) greying is progressive in nature (the total number and percentage of grey hairs increases over time), and (iv) the proportion of white hairs reaches high levels in old age, although some hairs can retain pigmentation until death, particularly among certain body regions (Trueb and Tobin, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Greying routinely starts between 20 and 50 years of age.
source: As basic tenets for this model, it is established that (i) the onset of human hair greying is not yet underway and rarely begins in childhood, (ii) greying routinely starts between 20 and 50 years of age, (iii) greying is progressive in nature (the total number and percentage of grey hairs increases over time), and (iv) the proportion of white hairs reaches high levels in old age, although some hairs can retain pigmentation until death, particularly among certain body regions (Trueb and Tobin, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Greying is progressive in nature (the total number and percentage of grey hairs increases over time).
source: As basic tenets for this model, it is established that (i) the onset of human hair greying is not yet underway and rarely begins in childhood, (ii) greying routinely starts between 20 and 50 years of age, (iii) greying is progressive in nature (the total number and percentage of grey hairs increases over time), and (iv) the proportion of white hairs reaches high levels in old age, although some hairs can retain pigmentation until death, particularly among certain body regions (Trueb and Tobin, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: The proportion of white hairs reaches high levels in old age, although some hairs can retain pigmentation until death, particularly among certain body regions.
source: As basic tenets for this model, it is established that (i) the onset of human hair greying is not yet underway and rarely begins in childhood, (ii) greying routinely starts between 20 and 50 years of age, (iii) greying is progressive in nature (the total number and percentage of grey hairs increases over time), and (iv) the proportion of white hairs reaches high levels in old age, although some hairs can retain pigmentation until death, particularly among certain body regions (Trueb and Tobin, 2010).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: Age-related greying is naturally reversible in isolated hair follicles, at least temporarily and in individual hair shafts, and may be acutely triggered by stressful life experiences.
source: Additionally, our findings demonstrate that (v) age-related greying is naturally reversible in isolated hair follicles, at least temporarily and in individual HS, and may be acutely triggered by stressful life experiences, the removal of which can trigger reversal.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: The removal of stressful life experiences can trigger reversal of hair greying.
source: Additionally, our findings demonstrate that (v) age-related greying is naturally reversible in isolated hair follicles, at least temporarily and in individual HS, and may be acutely triggered by stressful life experiences, the removal of which can trigger reversal.
evidence: This is a finding from the current study.

claim: The satisfactory model for hair greying has three components: an 'aging factor' that progressively accumulates, a biological threshold beyond which hairs undergo depigmentation, and a 'stress factor' that acutely but reversibly increases the aging factor.
source: Aiming for the simplest model that accounts for these known features of hair greying dynamics, we found a satisfactory model with three components (Figure 5B): (1) an 'aging factor' that progressively accumulates within each hair follicle, based on the fact that biological aging is more accurately modeled with the accumulation of damage, rather than a decline in stem cells or other reserves (Kinzina et al., 2019); (2) a biological threshold, beyond which hairs undergo depigmentation (i.e. greying), characterizing the transition between the dark and white states in the same HS; and (3) a 'stress factor' that acutely but reversibly increases the aging factor during a stressful event.
evidence: This is a description of the computational model developed in the study.

claim: The model's predicted hair population behavior across the lifespan is consistent with expected normal human hair greying dynamics.
source: We find that the model's predicted hair population behavior (% of white HSs on a person's head over time) across the lifespan is consistent with expected normal human hair greying dynamics (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: The model recapitulates the expected between-hair heterogeneity of greying within an individual, producing the common admixture of white and pigmented hairs or 'salt and pepper' phenotype in middle-age.
source: Thus, this model recapitulates the expected between-hair heterogeneity of greying within an individual, producing the common admixture of white and pigmented hairs or 'salt and pepper' phenotype in middle-age.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: A higher rate of accumulation of the aging factor or a lower threshold naturally accounts for earlier onset of greying.
source: A higher rate of accumulation of the aging factor (higher slope for each hair) or a lower threshold naturally accounts for earlier onset of greying.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: Greater hair-to-hair heterogeneity in the rate of aging between hair follicles is associated with earlier onset of greying.
source: In addition, our model reveals that within a person, greater hair-to-hair heterogeneity in the rate of aging between HFs, modeled as the standard deviation of slope across hairs, also influences the onset of greying. Greater heterogeneity between HFs allows for earlier onset of greying, whereas decreasing hair-to-hair variation (i.e. lower heterogeneity) is associated with a 'youthful' later onset of greying (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: Increased cell-to-cell heterogeneity is a conserved feature of aging.
source: Interestingly, this unpredicted result aligns with the notion that increased cell-to-cell heterogeneity is a conserved feature of aging (Bahar et al., 2006; Enge et al., 2017; Martinez-Jimenez et al., 2017) and that biological heterogeneity can predict all-cause mortality in humans (Patel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Biological heterogeneity can predict all-cause mortality in humans.
source: Interestingly, this unpredicted result aligns with the notion that increased cell-to-cell heterogeneity is a conserved feature of aging (Bahar et al., 2006; Enge et al., 2017; Martinez-Jimenez et al., 2017) and that biological heterogeneity can predict all-cause mortality in humans (Patel et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The model predicts transitory, or temporary reversible events of greying.
source: Using parameter values that yield the average onset and rate of greying, we then simulated the influence of acute psychosocial stressors, either early in life before the onset of greying, or later once grey HSs have begun to accumulate. Similar to our data, the model also predicts transitory, or temporary reversible events of greying (see Figure 3D).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: Transitory greying events do not affect all hairs, only those that are close to the threshold at the time of stress exposure undergo greying.
source: Transitory greying events do not affect all hairs, only those that are close to the threshold at the time of stress exposure undergo greying.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: Hairs whose cumulative aging factors are substantially lower than threshold do not show stress-induced greying.
source: Hairs whose cumulative aging factors are substantially lower than threshold do not show stress-induced greying (a 5-year-old is unlikely to get grey hairs from stress, but a 30-year-old can) (Figure 5E–F).
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: Grey hairs far above threshold are not affected by periods of psychosocial stress.
source: Similarly, grey hairs far above threshold are not affected by periods of psychosocial stress.
evidence: This is a result from the computational model.

claim: The model accounts for both the overall hair greying dynamics across the lifespan, and how a stressor (or its removal) may precipitate (or cause reversal of) greying in hairs whose aging factor is close to the greying threshold.
source: Thus, our model accounts for both the overall hair greying dynamics across the lifespan, and how a stressor (or its removal) may precipitate (or cause reversal of) greying in hairs whose aging factor is close to the greying threshold.
evidence: This is a summary of the computational model's capabilities.

claim: Hair pigmentation pattern data from individuals could be used in models to formulate predictions about future greying trajectories.
source: We speculate that this simulation opens an attractive possibility whereby HPP data from individuals could be used in models to formulate predictions about future greying trajectories, and to use HPPs and hair population greying behavior to track the effectiveness of behavioral and/or therapeutic interventions aimed at modifying human aging.
evidence: This is speculation about future applications of the model.

claim: Hairs among the same scalp regions may exhibit more similar hair pigmentation patterns than hairs sampled from different regions.
source: Extending our high-resolution quantitative digitization approach to hundreds of randomly sampled dark non-transitioning hairs from different scalp regions in the same individuals, we also show that fully dark (i.e. non-greying) HSs exhibit mostly unique HPPs, but that hairs among the same scalp regions may exhibit more similar HPPs than hairs sampled from different regions (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Stenn and Paus, 2001).
evidence: This is observational data from the study.

claim: The regional segregation of hair pigmentation patterns may reflect well-recognized regional differences in the rate of hair shaft formation.
source: This may in part be influenced by the migration of stem cells during embryogenesis to different parts of the scalp, or by other unknown factors. This preliminary extension of the HPP methodology provides a foundation for future studies. Moreover, the regional segregation of HPPs may reflect well-recognized regional differences in the rate of HS formation (Robbins, 2012).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The approach to quantify hair pigmentation patterns demonstrates rapid greying transitions and their natural transitory reversal within individual human hair follicles at a higher frequency and with different kinetics than had previously been appreciated.
source: Our approach to quantify HPPs demonstrates rapid greying transitions and their natural transitory reversal within individual human hair follicles at a higher frequency and with different kinetics than had previously been appreciated.
evidence: This is a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The literature generally assumes pigment production in the hair follicle pigmentary unit to be a continuous process for the entire duration of an anagen cycle.
source: The literature generally assumes pigment production in the HFPU to be a continuous process for the entire duration of an anagen cycle, but here we document a complete switch-on/off phenomena during a single anagen cycle.
evidence: This is a statement about existing literature and the novelty of the current findings.

claim: The study documents a complete switch-on/off phenomena of pigment production during a single anagen cycle.
source: The literature generally assumes pigment production in the HFPU to be a continuous process for the entire duration of an anagen cycle, but here we document a complete switch-on/off phenomena during a single anagen cycle.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: The proteomic features of hair greying directly implicate multiple metabolic pathways that are both reversible in nature and sensitive to stress-related neuroendocrine factors.
source: The proteomic features of hair greying directly implicate multiple metabolic pathways that are both reversible in nature and sensitive to stress-related neuroendocrine factors.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic findings.

claim: The proteomic findings provide a plausible biological basis for the rapid reversibility of greying and its association with psychological factors.
source: Therefore, this result provides a plausible biological basis for the rapid reversibility of greying and its association with psychological factors, and also supports the possibility that this process could be targeted pharmacologically.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic findings.

claim: The hair greying process could potentially be targeted pharmacologically.
source: Therefore, this result provides a plausible biological basis for the rapid reversibility of greying and its association with psychological factors, and also supports the possibility that this process could be targeted pharmacologically.
evidence: This is speculation based on the findings.

claim: Melanogenesis is known to both involve and respond to oxidative stress, a byproduct of mitochondrial metabolic processes and driver of senescence.
source: Melanogenesis is also known to both involve and respond to oxidative stress, a byproduct of mitochondrial metabolic processes (Balaban et al., 2005) and driver of senescence (Vizioli et al., 2020).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Alterations in energy metabolism are a major contributor to other disease-related aging features.
source: Moreover, alterations in energy metabolism are a major contributor to other disease-related aging features (Kennedy et al., 2014), including lifespan regulation (Jang et al., 2018; Latorre-Pellicer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The upregulation of specific components related to mitochondrial energy metabolism in white hairs suggests that energy metabolism regulates not only hair growth but also hair follicle greying biology.
source: The upregulation of specific components related to mitochondrial energy metabolism in white hairs suggests that energy metabolism regulates not only hair growth as previously demonstrated (Flores et al., 2017; Mancino et al., 2020; Vidali et al., 2014) but also HF greying biology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic findings and citations to previous research.

claim: Fatty acid synthesis by FASN and transport by CPT1a are sufficient drivers of cell senescence.
source: Our findings demonstrating an upregulation of the fatty acid synthesis and metabolism machinery resonate particularly strongly with recent work demonstrating that fatty acid synthesis by FASN (Fafián-Labora et al., 2019) and transport by CPT1a (Seok et al., 2020) are sufficient drivers of cell senescence, and that fatty acid metabolism regulates melanocyte aging biology (Tang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Fatty acid metabolism regulates melanocyte aging biology.
source: Our findings demonstrating an upregulation of the fatty acid synthesis and metabolism machinery resonate particularly strongly with recent work demonstrating that fatty acid synthesis by FASN (Fafián-Labora et al., 2019) and transport by CPT1a (Seok et al., 2020) are sufficient drivers of cell senescence, and that fatty acid metabolism regulates melanocyte aging biology (Tang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: The reversal of hair greying is not an isolated case of 'rejuvenation' in mammals.
source: Although surprising, the reversal of hair greying is not an isolated case of 'rejuvenation' in mammals.
evidence: This is a statement contextualizing the findings within broader biological phenomena.

claim: Exposing aged mice to young blood in parabiosis experiments triggers the reversal of age-related molecular, structural and functional impairments.
source: In vivo, exposing aged mice to young blood in parabiosis experiments (Rebo et al., 2016; Villeda et al., 2014) or diluting age-related factors in old animals (Mehdipour et al., 2020) triggers the reversal of age-related molecular, structural and functional impairments.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: In human cells, quantitative biological age indicators such as telomere length and DNA methylation exhibit temporary reversal in response to exercise and dietary interventions.
source: In human cells, quantitative biological age indicators such as telomere length (Puterman et al., 2018) and DNA methylation (Fahy et al., 2019) also exhibit temporary reversal in response to exercise and dietary interventions.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: The reversibility of greying in aging human hair follicles is consistent with the observed reversibility of human skin aging in vivo when aged human skin is xenotransplanted onto young nude mice.
source: Moreover, the reversibility of greying in aging human HFs demonstrated by our data is also consistent with the observed reversibility of human skin aging in vivo when aged human skin is xenotransplanted onto young nude mice (Gilhar et al., 1991a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Skin 'rejuvenation' is associated with a marked increase in the number of melanocytes in human epidermis.
source: Notably this skin 'rejuvenation' is associated with a marked increase in the number of melanocytes in human epidermis (Gilhar et al., 1991b), suggesting plasticity of the melanocyte compartment.
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous research.

claim: Human aging is not a linear, fixed biological process but may, at least in part, be halted or even temporarily reversed.
source: Therefore, our HPP data and simulation model adds to a growing body of evidence demonstrating that human aging is not a linear, fixed biological process but may, at least in part, be halted or even temporarily reversed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current findings and previous research.

claim: A notable finding from both proteomics experiments is the bias toward upregulation rather than the loss of proteins in depigmented grey hair shafts.
source: A notable finding from both proteomics experiments is the bias toward upregulation rather than the loss of proteins in depigmented grey HS.
evidence: This is a summary of the proteomic findings.

claim: Hair greying is an actively regulated process within the hair follicle pigmentary unit.
source: As noted above, this may reflect the fact that hair greying is an actively regulated process within the HPFU, and that aging is not marked by a loss, but rather an increase in heterogeneity and biological complexity (Bahar et al., 2006; Enge et al., 2017; LaRocca et al., 2020; Martinez-Jimenez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference based on the proteomic findings and citations to previous research.

claim: Aging is not marked by a loss, but rather an increase in heterogeneity and biological complexity.
source: As noted above, this may reflect the fact that hair greying is an actively regulated process within the HPFU, and that aging is not marked by a loss, but rather an increase in heterogeneity and biological complexity (Bahar et al., 2006; Enge et al., 2017; LaRocca et al., 2020; Martinez-Jimenez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Relative to the youthful state, quiescent and senescent cells exhibit upregulation of various secreted factors and elevated metabolic activities.
source: Relative to the youthful state, quiescent and senescent cells exhibit upregulation of various secreted factors (van Deursen, 2014), as well as elevated metabolic activities (Lemons et al., 2010), rather than global downregulation of cellular activities.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Age-related senescence markers naturally occur stochastically for DNA methylation changes across the genome and among cells heterogeneously scattered within tissues in mice.
source: Moreover, similar to the macroscopic appearance of hair greying, age-related senescence markers naturally occur stochastically for DNA methylation changes across the genome (Franzen et al., 2017) and among cells heterogeneously scattered within tissues in mice (Baker et al., 2016; Omori et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous research.
